name: DROVNE Rocca
author: DROVNE

sections.description:
DROVNE Rocca protects a WordPress site with a few focused tools. Each one has its own switch, and the plugin never contacts an outside server.

Login protection

  • Locks out an IP address after too many failed logins, counted on the login form, XML-RPC and application passwords.
  • Lockouts grow: after repeated lockouts within a day, the next one lasts hours instead of minutes.
  • An allowlist of addresses and ranges, IPv4 and IPv6, that are never locked out, with a button to add your own address.
  • A list of the addresses locked out now, with an Unlock button.
  • The same error for a wrong username and a wrong password, so the form does not reveal which accounts exist.

Two-factor authentication

  • A code from an authenticator app at every login, such as Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis or 2FAS. Codes follow the TOTP standard (RFC 6238).
  • Each user sets it up under Users > Two-factor by scanning a QR code. The QR code is drawn by the plugin itself, so the key never reaches an outside service.
  • Ten single-use backup codes for a lost phone. Only their hashes are stored, and the app key is stored encrypted.
  • Require it for chosen roles: those users set up their app at their next login, before they get in.
  • The password alone never starts a session: the code is asked for before any login cookie is sent. Wrong codes count toward the login lockout.
  • Programs that log in through XML-RPC use an application password, as core provides.
  • Administrators can turn it off for a user who lost both the phone and the backup codes.

Firewall

  • Checks every request before other plugins load, from a small must-use plugin that Rocca writes when you turn the firewall on and removes when you turn it off.
  • Rules, each with its own switch: SQL injection, script injection, path traversal and file inclusion in the address; probes for .env, .git, configuration backups and database dumps; known vulnerability scanners; request methods WordPress does not use.
  • Only the address, method, address bar and user agent are checked. Form data is not, so posts and comments about code are never blocked.
  • Block mode, or log-only mode to try the rules on your site first.
  • Blocked addresses and ranges, and an optional limit of requests per minute per address.
  • A log of the latest matches. A blocked visitor sees a short reference that you can find in the log.
  • An emergency switch in wp-config.php if a rule ever locks you out.
  • The rules are written into the plugin and change only with plugin updates: no outside rule feed.

Activity log

  • Records who did what and from which address: logins and logouts, lockouts, password resets, two-factor and application password changes.
  • Users created, deleted, given another role, or with a new email address or password. Passwords are never stored.
  • Plugins and themes installed, updated, activated, deactivated, switched or deleted, and WordPress updates.
  • Changes to important settings, such as the site address, the admin email, registration and the default role, with the value before and after, and every change to Rocca’s own settings.
  • Filter by kind of action and by user, page through older entries and download a CSV file.
  • Written with one database query at the end of a request, and deleted after 90 days by default.

File checks

  • Every day, a background check fingerprints the code files of WordPress, plugins, themes, must-use plugins and uploads: PHP, JavaScript, .htaccess and .user.ini.
  • The first check becomes the baseline. Later checks list changed, new and missing files, and you accept the ones you recognize.
  • PHP in the uploads folder is always listed until you accept it, even on the first check: uploads should hold no code.
  • Updates made from the dashboard refresh the baseline of what they replaced, so a normal update raises no alarm.
  • An email to the site administrator when a check finds something new.
  • No outside data: the baseline is your own site, taken at a time you trust. Rocca never changes or deletes a file.

Hardening

  • Turns off the plugin and theme file editors.
  • XML-RPC: allowed, without logins and pingbacks, or off entirely.
  • Hides usernames from visitors: author numbers, the REST user list, oEmbed and the users sitemap.
  • Removes the WordPress version from the page head and feeds.
  • Sends X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options and Referrer-Policy on public pages, unless they are already set.

Behind a proxy

By default Rocca uses the address of the direct connection. If your site sits behind Cloudflare or another proxy, choose the header it sets on the Settings page, which shows the value of each header for your own request.

Privacy

Rocca stores what it needs in your own database, and each kind of record is deleted after a period you choose:

  • A failed login: the IP address, the name typed and the time. 30 days by default.
  • A request stopped or logged by the firewall: the IP address, method, address requested, user agent and time. 30 days by default.
  • The activity log: the username, IP address and time of each action. 90 days by default. An erasure request removes the person’s username and address from their entries and keeps the events.
  • Two-factor: an encrypted app key and hashes of the backup codes, stored with the user’s account until two-factor is turned off.

Rocca adds a suggested paragraph to the privacy policy guide and supports the WordPress personal data export and erase tools.

DROVNE Rocca is an independent plugin. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by WordPress or Automattic.
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate the plugin. Login protection, hardening, the activity log and the daily file check start right away; the first file check makes the baseline.
  2. Open Rocca in the admin menu and check the Overview.
  3. If the Overview warns that your address is private, choose your proxy header on the Settings page before anything else.
  4. Set up two-factor for your own account under Users > Two-factor, then choose on Rocca > Two-factor which roles must use it.
  5. Turn on the firewall on Rocca > Firewall. On a busy site, start with “Only log it” for a few days and look at the matches.
sections.faq:
I locked myself out. What now?

Wait until the lockout ends, or log in from another network and press Unlock on the Login protection page. If you cannot wait, rename the plugin folder over FTP or your host’s file manager: WordPress then deactivates it.

I lost my phone. How do I log in?

Enter one of your backup codes instead of the app code, then set up your new phone under Users > Two-factor. Without backup codes, ask an administrator to turn two-factor off on your profile. If you are the only administrator, rename the plugin folder over FTP or your host’s file manager to deactivate it, log in, and rename it back.

What happens if I change the security keys in wp-config.php?

The app keys are encrypted with a key made from them, so they can no longer be read: users log in with a backup code and set up their app again. To keep the app keys across a change, define DROVNE_RC_SECRET_KEY in wp-config.php with a long random value before users set up their apps.

A firewall rule blocks something my site needs. What now?

Switch the firewall to log-only mode, or turn off that rule on the Firewall page. If you cannot reach the dashboard, add define( ‘DROVNE_RC_FIREWALL_OFF’, true ); to wp-config.php, fix the setting, then remove the line. Addresses on the allowlist are never stopped.

Does the firewall replace a server firewall or a hosted firewall?

No. It sees only requests that reach WordPress, after the web server. Static files and pages served from a page cache never reach it.

Why not compare WordPress files with the official checksums?

Those come from WordPress.org, and Rocca contacts no outside server. The local baseline also covers premium plugins and your own code, which have no public checksums. If the site was already infected before the first check, the baseline includes the infection: start on a clean copy, or look at the files the first check lists in uploads.

Does Rocca send data anywhere?

No. Everything is stored in your own database. The only message that leaves the site is the file check email, sent by your own site to its administration email address, and you can turn it off.

Will it slow my site down?

Public pages get a few filters and, with the firewall on, a handful of pattern checks on the address. The database is read on login requests, written when the firewall stops a request, and once per request only if you set a rate limit without a persistent object cache.
sections.changelog:
0.1.0

  • First version: login attempt limits with growing lockouts, allowlist, generic login errors, two-factor authentication with backup codes and required roles, a firewall that starts before other plugins, an activity log, daily file checks against a local baseline, hardening switches and security headers.

short_description: Light security suite: login limits, two-factor, firewall, activity log, file checks and hardening. Nothing contacts an outside server.
